cases.abstract: DROID addresses the joint demands of scene-diverse manipulation data and reproducible collection through a distributed dataset and a shared, portable robot platform. Across 13 institutions, collectors use VR teleoperation, calibrate cameras for each scene, and receive tasks randomly sampled from a feasible task list; periodic prompts vary viewpoints and scene conditions to broaden coverage. The release contains 76,000 successful episodes from 564 scenes in 52 buildings, together with collection and policy-training resources. Evaluation uses existing language-conditioned diffusion policies for six tasks at four locations on the shared hardware, holding the backbone fixed across training conditions. Co-training mixes successful DROID trajectories and in-domain demonstrations 50/50, with alternatives using in-domain data alone or an equal mixture with curated Open X-Embodiment data. DROID co-training yields mean success 22 percentage points above the next-best alternative in-distribution and 17 points above it on task-specific out-of-distribution variants. A size-matched subset comparison further supports a role for scene diversity on the challenging shifted tasks studied.
cases.methods: DROID uses a portable Franka Panda setup with external and wrist stereo cameras and VR teleoperation to keep collection reproducible across institutions while allowing scenes to change. Collectors calibrate cameras and list feasible tasks for each scene, then receive a randomly sampled task for each episode. Periodic prompts vary camera placement, lighting, clutter, or base position to broaden coverage rather than favor easy tasks. Evaluation trains separate language-conditioned diffusion policies for six tasks on the shared hardware, holding the backbone fixed across training conditions. DROID co-training mixes successful dataset trajectories with in-domain demonstrations 50/50; alternatives use in-domain data alone or a 50/50 mixture with curated Open X-Embodiment data. Ten rollouts per method and task setting compare success with perturbed initial robot and object positions and under task-specific shifts involving distractors, new manipulated objects, or camera placement.
cases.results: Across six tasks at four locations on DROID hardware, 50/50 co-training with successful DROID trajectories and in-domain demonstrations yields mean success 22 percentage points above the next-best alternative in-distribution and 17 points above it on task-specific out-of-distribution variants. Comparators use the same policy backbone with in-domain data alone or a 50/50 mixture of in-domain and curated Open X-Embodiment data. Each method and task setting is evaluated with ten rollouts. To examine scene coverage separately from subset size, a further comparison uses 7,362 successful demonstrations in each subset and equal mixing with in-domain data. A uniformly sampled, more scene-diverse subset performs better on the challenging shifted tasks studied than one drawn from the 20 most represented scenes. This comparison supports a role for scene diversity beyond demonstration count, although it does not isolate every other difference between the subsets.

notes.abstract: Preserved the dataset and collection platform as joint resource contributions (D01-D04, D09). Read-back connects scene variation under common hardware to task-scoped utility (D05-D08), without implying a new learning algorithm or an isolated causal effect of diversity.
notes.methods: D01-D02 support reproducible hardware with deliberate collection variation; D05-D07 support the evaluation procedure. Read-back identifies task sampling, matched backbones, data mixtures, and distinct evaluation shifts. Successful trajectories supply DROID co-training, and the rollout count applies to the main comparison.
notes.results: D05-D07 anchor the six-task comparison and percentage-point gains over the next-best alternative. D08 anchors the separate size-matched diversity check. Read-back retains in-domain co-training and hardware scope while treating broader scene coverage as supported, not uniquely causal.

cases.abstract: SIMPLER is a simulated evaluation framework for comparing policies trained on real robot data, emphasizing relative performance and behavioral differences rather than exact physical success rates. To align action effects, it replays actions from existing demonstrations and tunes controller stiffness and damping against end-effector trajectory mismatch. Visual Matching addresses visual mismatch by compositing simulated robots and interactive objects onto an inpainted real-scene background and adjusting their textures. The framework also measures ranking errors using Mean Maximum Rank Violation, which averages each policy's largest misranking margin in real-world success rates. For six checkpoints across three Google Robot task groups, Visual Matching yields average MMRV of 0.056, compared with 0.143 for Variant Aggregation over randomized visual environments and 0.375 for validation action MSE. Simulation also suggests greater arm-texture sensitivity for Octo-Base than RT-1-X, a relative difference supported by new physical arm-wrapping experiments. These comparisons support simulation as a signal for policy ranking and robustness analysis within the evaluated rigid-body setups.
cases.methods: SIMPLER pairs simulated and physical evaluations of policies trained on real data in Google Robot and WidowX setups, mainly for rigid-body tasks. It aligns action effects by replaying actions from existing real demonstrations and tuning controller stiffness and damping through simulated annealing to reduce end-effector translation and rotation mismatch; no new demonstrations are collected for this step. Visual Matching composites segmented simulated robots and interactive objects with an inpainted real-scene background, then adjusts or projects textures to align their appearance. Variant Aggregation instead averages outcomes over randomized visual environments. To assess whether simulated outcomes preserve physical policy ordering, Mean Maximum Rank Violation averages each policy's largest misranking margin in real-world success rates. Pearson correlation provides a complementary measure, since correlation alone can misrepresent nonlinear but order-preserving performance or noisy comparisons within a narrow range.
cases.results: For six policy checkpoints across three Google Robot task groups, Visual Matching provides better agreement with physical policy ordering than Variant Aggregation or validation action MSE. Average Mean Maximum Rank Violation is 0.056, compared with 0.143 and 0.375 for the two alternatives, respectively; mean Pearson correlation is also higher, at 0.924 versus 0.778 and 0.308. The MMRV contrast favors Visual Matching when ranking errors are judged by the physical performance gap between misordered policies. A separate check connects simulated robustness patterns to physical behavior: Octo-Base appears more sensitive to arm texture than RT-1-X in simulation, and new real-world arm-wrapping experiments support that relative sensitivity. Together, these comparisons support simulation as an informative ranking and behavioral evaluation signal for the tested policies and rigid-body setups, rather than exact success-rate reproduction.

notes.abstract: S01-S05 support the framework, alignment operations, and margin-aware metric; S07 and S09 support ranking and sensitivity comparisons. Read-back retains both framework and metric contributions, distinguishes ranking error from robot success, and scopes the positive claim to evaluated rigid-body setups.
notes.methods: S02-S06 connect action alignment, visual alignment, and paired policy evaluation. Read-back preserves action replay from existing demonstrations, robot and object appearance matching, and worst-margin averaging. Correlation is complementary, and the no-new-demonstration condition remains confined to controller identification.
notes.results: S07 anchors both ranking measures and their Google Robot comparison; S09 anchors the physically checked arm-texture sensitivity. Read-back interprets MMRV through misranking margins rather than success gains and restricts the secondary finding to the named policies and tested conditions.
